summary: WISE 0855-0714 is a known brown dwarf, the coldest one catalogued, only 7.3 light-years away. WANDERERS measured a shift of 131 arcseconds between 2010 and 2026. That is about 8.24 arcseconds per year, within 1.1% of the catalogue value. SPHEREx saw it bright at 4 to 4.75 microns but did not detect it at 3.3 microns. So the methane ratio is only a lower limit, above 4, which fits a very cold object. Gaia has no match. Also, 41 of 150 spectrum points are flagged. Confidence is high.

qa.q: Why do we think this is what the card says?
qa.a: Three checks support the card. It moved 131 arcseconds since 2010, which matches the catalogue speed within 1.1%. Such fast motion means it is very close, and the literature gives 7.3 light-years. It is bright at 4 to 4.75 microns but undetected at 3.3 microns, where methane absorbs. That gap means a very cold brown dwarf. Gaia cannot see it, and 41 of 150 spectrum points are flagged.

qa.q: What would make you less sure?
qa.a: Several things make me less sure. 41 of the 150 spectrum points are flagged. The 3.3 µm signal is weak, 0.117 ± 0.047 mJy, so the methane ratio is only a lower limit. Some fluxes near 4 and 4.9 µm are near zero or negative, which is a sign of noise. The north-south motion is 823 milliarcseconds per year, against 673 in the catalogue. Gaia cannot check it.

qa.q: Why use both WISE and SPHEREx?
qa.a: WISE pictured this sky around 2010, and SPHEREx looked again in 2025 and 2026. Over that 16-year gap the brown dwarf moved 131 arcseconds, about 21 SPHEREx pixels. A shift that big is easy to measure: 8.24 arcseconds per year, close to the catalogue value of 8.15. SPHEREx also gives a 150-point spectrum. It shows a deep methane dip at 3.3 microns, where SPHEREx could not detect the dwarf at all. Note that 41 points are flagged.
